questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: What is the SI unit of moment of inertia?

text_solutions: Moment of inertia \( I = \sum m_i r_i^2 \) has units of mass times distance squared, so the SI unit is \( \text{kg m}^2 \).

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: A \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) object moves with a velocity of \( 3 \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} - 2 \, \hat{\mathbf{j}} \, \text{m/s} \). What is the magnitude of the velocity of its center of mass?

text_solutions:
For a single object, the center of mass velocity equals the object’s velocity.

Magnitude = \( \sqrt{(3)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 4} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.6 \, \text{m/s} \).

qns_content.text: A \( 5 \, \text{kg} \) block slides down an inclined plane with a constant velocity of \( 2 \, \text{m/s} \). What is the velocity of the center of mass of the block?

text_solutions:
For a single body in pure translational motion, the velocity of the center of mass is the same as the velocity of the body.

Given: \( v = 2 \, \text{m/s} \).

Thus, \( \mathbf{V} = 2 \, \text{m/s} \) (direction along the incline).

qns_content.text: What is the condition for a rigid body to have zero angular acceleration?

text_solutions: Angular acceleration is zero when the net torque is zero (\( \mathbf{\tau} = I \mathbf{\alpha} \)), as torque drives rotational change.

qns_content.text: Which physical quantity is defined as \( \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} \) for a particle?

text_solutions: Angular momentum of a particle is defined as \( \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} \), where \( \mathbf{r} \) is the position vector and \( \mathbf{p} \) is the linear momentum.

qns_content.text: Why can a rigid body not deform under the influence of forces in theoretical mechanics?

options.text: Because it is an idealization with fixed distances

text_solutions: In theoretical mechanics, a rigid body is an idealization where inter-particle distances are fixed, preventing deformation and allowing focus on rotational and translational motion only.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: Why does a symmetric body rotating about its symmetry axis have angular momentum aligned with the axis?

text_solutions: Symmetry ensures perpendicular components of angular momentum cancel out, leaving \( \mathbf{L} = I \mathbf{\omega} \) aligned with the axis of rotation.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: A uniform rod of length \( 2 \, \text{m} \) and mass \( 4 \, \text{kg} \) lies along the x-axis with its left end at the origin. What is the position vector of its center of mass?

text_solutions:
For a uniform rod, the center of mass is at its geometric center.

Length = \( 2 \, \text{m} \), so the center is at \( 1 \, \text{m} \) from the origin along the x-axis.

Position vector: \( \mathbf{R} = 1 \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 0 \, \hat{\mathbf{j}} + 0 \, \hat{\mathbf{k}} = 1 \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} \, \text{m} \).

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: In rotational motion, what is the relationship between linear velocity and angular velocity for a particle?

text_solutions: The linear velocity \( v \) of a particle in rotational motion is related to angular velocity \( \omega \) by \( v = \omega r \), where \( r \) is the perpendicular distance from the axis.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: For a body rotating about a fixed axis, what is true about particles on the axis?

text_solutions: Particles on the axis of rotation have a perpendicular distance \( r = 0 \) from the axis, so their linear velocity \( v = \omega r = 0 \), meaning they remain stationary.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: Which of the following is true about the angular velocity of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?

options.text: It varies with distance from the axis
It is the same for all particles in the body
It is zero for points farthest from the axis
It depends on the mass of each particle

text_solutions: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, all particles have the same angular velocity, regardless of their distance from the axis, as it’s a property of the body’s rotation as a whole.

qns_content.text: A uniform rectangular plate of dimensions \( 3 \, \text{m} \times 5 \, \text{m} \) and mass \( 12 \, \text{kg} \) has one corner at \( (1, 1) \) along the x- and y-axes. What is the position of its center of mass?

text_solutions:
For a uniform rectangle, the center of mass is at the centroid.

Vertices: \( (1, 1), (4, 1), (1, 6), (4, 6) \).

CM: \( X = 1 + \frac{3}{2} = 2.5 \), \( Y = 1 + \frac{5}{2} = 3.5 \). Position: \( (2.5, 3.5) \, \text{m} \).

qns_content.text: A \( 4 \, \text{kg} \) block moves with a velocity of \( -2 \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3 \, \hat{\mathbf{j}} \, \text{m/s} \). What is the magnitude of the velocity of its center of mass?

text_solutions:
For a single object, the center of mass velocity equals the object’s velocity.

Magnitude = \( \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (3)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.6 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

qns_content.text: Which of the following best defines a rigid body?

options.text: A body that can only undergo translational motion
A body with a fixed shape where distances between particles do not change
A body that deforms under external forces

text_solutions: A rigid body is one where the distances between all pairs of particles remain constant, even under the influence of forces. This is an idealization, as real bodies deform slightly, but it’s a key assumption in rotational dynamics.

text_solutions: If the net external torque is zero (\( \frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt} = \mathbf{\tau} = 0 \)), angular momentum is conserved, and for a fixed moment of inertia, angular velocity remains constant.

text_solutions: For mechanical equilibrium, both translational and rotational equilibrium are required: the net force (\( \sum \mathbf{F} = 0 \)) and net torque (\( \sum \mathbf{\tau} = 0 \)) must be zero.

qns_content.text: What is the effect of doubling the radius of a rotating disk on its moment of inertia, assuming mass remains constant?

text_solutions: For a disk, \( I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 \). Doubling \( R \) increases \( R^2 \) by a factor of 4, so \( I \) increases by a factor of 4 if \( M \) is constant.

options.text: Because perpendicular distance from the axis changes

text_solutions: Torque depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force (\( \tau = r F \sin \theta \)), so the point of application changes \( r \), altering the torque.

text_solutions:
For a single object, the center of mass velocity equals the object’s velocity.

Magnitude = \( \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 4} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.39 \, \text{m/s} \).

qns_content.text: Why is the angular momentum of a symmetric rigid body about a fixed axis often aligned with the axis?

text_solutions: For a symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed axis (a symmetry axis), the perpendicular components of angular momentum cancel out due to symmetry, leaving \( \mathbf{L} = I \mathbf{\omega} \) aligned with the axis.

qns_content.text: A uniform triangular lamina has vertices at \( (0, 0) \), \( (6, 0) \), and \( (0, 8) \). What are the coordinates of its center of mass?

text_solutions:
For a uniform triangular lamina, the center of mass is at the centroid, given by the average of the vertices.

\( X = \frac{0 + 6 + 0}{3} = 2 \), \( Y = \frac{0 + 0 + 8}{3} = \frac{8}{3} \approx 2.67 \, \text{m} \).

Coordinates: \( (2, \frac{8}{3}) \).
